lessons.title: The mean is a balance point

sections.title: Start with a question
sections.text: Four study sessions lasted 2, 4, 4, and 6 hours. We want one number describing their center, but we also want to know what that number hides. The mean shares the total equally among observations. For n observations, the subscript i labels each value; the summation sign means “add these terms.”
sections.example: Here n = 4 and the total is 16 hours, so the mean is 4 hours. The datasets {4,4,4,4} and {2,4,4,6} share this mean, despite different variation.

sections.title: Deviations carry direction
sections.text: A deviation is an observation minus the mean. Negative deviations lie below the center; positive deviations lie above it. Our four deviations are −2, 0, 0, and 2 hours. Their sum is zero. This happens for every dataset, not just symmetric ones.
sections.example: For {1,2,9}, the mean is 4. Deviations −3, −2, and 5 still sum to zero. A mean need not be an observed value.

sections.title: What does the mean minimize?
sections.text: Suppose you choose another center c. Write each deviation from c as a deviation from the mean plus the displacement of the mean from c. Expand the squares. The cross term vanishes because deviations from the mean sum to zero. The remaining term is nonnegative, and is zero exactly when c equals the mean.
sections.example: For {2,4,4,6}, squared distances from 4 sum to 8. From 5 they sum to 12 = 8 + 4(4−5)². The mean uniquely minimizes the sum of squared distances.

sections.title: Use the center with judgment
sections.text: The mean is sensitive to extreme observations because each observation contributes to the total. The median is the middle ordered value (or mean of the two middle values) and can better describe a typical observation in a strongly skewed dataset. Neither is universally superior: match the summary to the question.
sections.example: For incomes {30,32,33,35,200}, the mean is 66 and median 33. The mean is useful for the total divided across people, but it does not describe a typical income well.

sections.title: Why square the deviations?
sections.text: Averaging signed deviations always gives zero. Squaring removes cancellation, gives larger deviations more weight, and leads to useful algebra. Absolute deviations also measure spread, but have different mathematical properties. Variance uses squared deviations; it is not the only possible measure of spread.
sections.example: If {2,4,4,6} is the entire population of interest, squared deviations are 4,0,0,4. Population variance is 8/4 = 2 hours².

sections.title: Return to the original units
sections.text: Standard deviation is the nonnegative square root of variance. If measurements are in hours, variance is in hours squared and standard deviation is in hours. Standard deviation is a scale of variation around the mean, not the literal average absolute distance.
sections.example: The population standard deviation of {2,4,4,6} is √2 ≈ 1.414 hours. Do not report 2 hours as the standard deviation.

sections.title: A sample estimates a larger population
sections.text: When independent, identically distributed observations sample a population with finite variance, the sample mean is fitted to the same data. That fit makes deviations smaller on average than deviations from the true population mean. Dividing the squared deviations by n−1 corrects this downward bias in the variance estimate. It does not make the standard deviation itself unbiased.
sections.example: If {2,4,4,6} is a sample used to estimate a broader population, s² = 8/3 and s ≈ 1.633. The data did not change; the purpose of the calculation did.

sections.title: Why n−1 appears
sections.text: Because the deviations sum to zero, once n−1 of them are chosen, the last is determined. This explains the degrees of freedom. A stronger justification uses expectation: the sample mean has variance σ²/n, so fitting the mean removes one σ² of expected squared deviation. We will derive that variance-of-the-mean result in the sampling unit.
sections.example: Taking expectations gives nσ² − n(σ²/n) = (n−1)σ². Therefore E[s²] = σ². Independence, a common distribution, and finite variance matter.

lessons.title: Change the scale, keep the structure

sections.title: Shifting and rescaling
sections.text: Add a to every observation and multiply by b. The mean moves with the observations. Subtracting the new mean cancels the shift, leaving each deviation multiplied by b. Squaring multiplies variance by b²; taking the square root multiplies standard deviation by |b|.
sections.example: If Celsius temperatures have mean 20 and SD 3, Fahrenheit values Y = 32 + 1.8X have mean 68 and SD 5.4. Adding 32 contributes no variation.

sections.title: Measure position in standard deviations
sections.text: A z-score says how far an observation lies from its reference mean, measured in reference standard deviations. It has no units. Positive means above the mean; negative means below. Standardization requires positive standard deviation.
sections.example: A score of 85 in a population with mean 70 and SD 10 has z = 1.5. A score of 65 has z = −0.5.

sections.title: A z-score is not a percentile
sections.text: Standardizing a distribution changes its center and scale, not its shape. A skewed distribution stays skewed. A z-score alone cannot tell you the percentage below an observation; that requires distributional information. Rules based on a normal curve apply only when a normal model is appropriate.
sections.example: A value with z = 2 is two standard deviations above the mean. It is not automatically the 97.7th percentile. That percentile follows from a normal model, not from standardization itself.

sections.title: Connect the ideas
sections.text: Reconstruct the chain: the mean balances deviations; squared deviations quantify spread; standard deviation restores measurement units; standardization removes those units. Before a quiz, explain each link aloud, then work one example without notes.
sections.example: For the population {2,4,4,6}: μ = 4, σ² = 2, σ = √2. Standardized values are {−√2,0,0,√2}. They have population mean 0 and variance 1.

sections.title: Locate before you calculate
sections.text: Positive and negative numbers describe positions relative to a chosen zero. On a number line, numbers increase to the right. Absolute value measures distance from zero, so it is nonnegative. The opposite of a number reverses its direction; it does not necessarily make the number negative.
sections.example: A temperature of −7°C is lower than −2°C. Both are below zero, but −7 lies farther left. The distance between them is |−7−(−2)| = 5 degrees.

sections.title: Addition combines changes
sections.text: Adding a positive number moves right; adding a negative number moves left. Subtracting a number means adding its opposite. This rule is more dependable than “two negatives make a positive,” which can confuse subtraction with multiplication.
sections.example: −4 + 7 = 3. Also, −4 − (−7) = −4 + 7 = 3, while −4 + (−7) = −11. Identify the operation before applying a sign rule.

sections.title: Multiplication preserves arithmetic patterns
sections.text: Distributivity explains the sign rules. Since 3(2 + (−2)) = 0, the values 3·2 and 3·(−2) must be opposites. Repeating that reasoning with a negative multiplier gives a positive product for two negative factors.
sections.example: The first term is −6, so the second must be +6. This derives (−3)(−2) = 6 from distributivity rather than a slogan.

sections.title: Read the structure of an expression
sections.text: Evaluate parentheses, then powers, then multiplication and division from left to right, then addition and subtraction from left to right. Multiplication and division have equal priority. A minus sign outside a power is different from a negative base inside parentheses.

lessons.title: Fractions are numbers, not two integers

sections.title: Keep the size of the whole fixed
sections.text: A fraction a/b is a divided by b, with b nonzero. The denominator describes the size of each equal part; the numerator counts those parts. Multiplying numerator and denominator by the same nonzero number changes the name, not the value.
sections.example: Six eighths of one pizza is three quarters of that same pizza. Comparing fractions of differently sized pizzas requires knowing the whole.

sections.title: Add quantities measured in the same parts
sections.text: You can combine numerators only after expressing both fractions with a common denominator. Adding denominators changes the unit instead of counting it. Reduce a fraction by dividing both numerator and denominator by a common nonzero factor.
sections.example: 5/6 − 1/4 = 10/12 − 3/12 = 7/12. The incorrect answer 4/2 comes from subtracting denominators, which does not preserve the size of the parts.

sections.title: Multiplication scales; division asks how many
sections.text: Multiplying by 2/3 takes two thirds of a quantity. Dividing by a nonzero fraction reverses that scaling, so multiply by its reciprocal. Division by zero remains undefined. A product can be smaller than either positive factor when the factors lie between zero and one.
sections.example: There are three half-cups in 1½ cups: (3/2) ÷ (1/2) = 3. You invert the divisor, not the number being divided.

sections.title: An exponent counts factors
sections.text: For a positive integer n, aⁿ means n factors of a multiplied together. It does not mean a times n. When multiplying powers with the same base, combine their lists of factors. When raising a power to a power, repeat the whole list.
sections.example: 2³ · 2² = (2·2·2)(2·2) = 2⁵ = 32. By contrast, 2³ + 2² = 8 + 4 = 12; the product rule does not apply to addition.

sections.title: Extend the pattern carefully
sections.text: For a nonzero base, reducing the exponent by one divides the value by the base. This gives a⁰ = 1 and a negative exponent as a reciprocal. A negative exponent does not mean a negative answer.
sections.example: 10² = 100, 10¹ = 10, 10⁰ = 1, and 10⁻² = 0.01. Scientific notation 3.2 × 10⁴ means 32,000. We do not apply these reciprocal rules to a base of zero.

sections.title: A root reverses a power with a convention
sections.text: The square-root symbol denotes the nonnegative root. Solving an equation is a different task: both 5 and −5 solve x² = 25. Because square roots return nonnegative values, √(x²) = |x| for real x.
sections.example: √((-7)²) = √49 = 7, not −7. Also, √(9+16) = √25 = 5, whereas √9 + √16 = 7. Square roots do not distribute over addition.

sections.title: Ratios compare quantities
sections.text: A ratio compares by division; a difference compares by subtraction. If a recipe uses 2 cups of oats for every 3 cups of milk, doubling both quantities preserves the ratio. Adding the same amount to each generally does not.
sections.example: For 9 cups of milk, multiply both parts of 2:3 by 3, giving 6 cups of oats. The fraction of the mixture that is oats is 2/(2+3) = 2/5, not 2/3.

sections.title: A unit rate makes comparisons easier
sections.text: A rate compares quantities with different units. Divide to obtain the amount per one unit. In a proportional relationship y = kx, k is constant and zero input gives zero output. A fixed starting fee breaks proportionality even when the variable rate is constant.
sections.example: Six notebooks cost $15, so the price is $2.50 per notebook. At that constant unit price, ten cost $25. A taxi fare of $4 plus $2 per kilometer is linear but not proportional.

sections.title: Percent means per hundred
sections.text: Convert p percent to p/100 before multiplying. A percentage change is measured relative to a stated starting amount. Successive percentage changes use different bases, so equal increases and decreases do not usually cancel.
sections.example: A $60 item discounted by 20% costs 60(0.8) = $48. If $100 increases by 10% and then decreases by 10%, the result is 100(1.1)(0.9) = $99.

sections.title: An expression is a rule for a value
sections.text: A variable represents a number whose value may be unknown or may vary. An expression has a value once its variables are specified. An equation asserts that two expressions are equal. Substitution must preserve grouping, especially when substituting negative numbers.
sections.example: The expression 3x + 7 does not itself ask you to find x. The equation 3x + 7 = 22 does. Parentheses prevent sign mistakes when evaluating an expression.

sections.title: Like terms count the same thing
sections.text: The terms 3x and 5x share the same variable part, so their coefficients add. Terms such as x and x² represent different quantities and cannot be combined into one like term. Constants combine with constants.
sections.example: 4x + 3 − 2x + 7 = 2x + 10. But 4x + 3x² stays as two terms. At x=2 it equals 20, while 7x³ would equal 56, so that proposed simplification fails.

sections.title: Distribute to every term
sections.text: Multiplication distributes over addition and subtraction. A negative sign before parentheses acts as multiplication by −1. Factoring reverses distribution by identifying a common multiplier.
sections.example: −2(3x − 4) = −6x + 8. Also, 5 − (x + 2) = 5 − x − 2 = 3 − x. Testing a few values can disprove a proposed identity, but proving it for all values requires valid algebraic transformations.

sections.title: Solutions make a statement true
sections.text: Solving an equation means finding every allowed value that makes the equality true. Adding the same quantity to both sides or multiplying both sides by a nonzero number gives an equivalent equation. Do not divide by an expression that could be zero without considering that case.
sections.example: Check by substitution: 3(5) + 7 = 22. “Move 7 and change its sign” is shorthand for subtracting 7 from both sides; the balanced operation is the reason it works.

sections.title: Undo structure, not just symbols
sections.text: Distribute and collect like terms when needed. Then collect variable terms on one side and constants on the other. With fractions, multiplying every term on both sides by a common nonzero denominator can simplify the arithmetic.
sections.example: x/3 + 2 = 5 gives x/3 = 3 and x = 9. Alternatively, multiply every term by 3: x + 6 = 15. Multiplying only one term would change the equation.

sections.title: Not every equation has one solution
sections.text: If the variables cancel, inspect what remains. A true statement means every allowed real value is a solution. A false statement means there are no solutions. Neither case should be forced into “x = 0.”
sections.example: 2(x+1) = 2x+2 reduces to 2 = 2, true for every real x. But 2(x+1) = 2x+5 reduces to 2 = 5, so there is no solution.

sections.title: Translate a situation and check its meaning
sections.text: Define the variable with its units before writing an equation. An algebraic answer must also fit the situation, including restrictions such as nonnegative counts or whole numbers.
sections.example: A membership costs $12 plus $4 per visit. If the total is $40, let v be visits: 12 + 4v = 40. Then v = 7, a valid nonnegative integer. Check: 12 + 4(7) = 40.

lessons.title: Describe a whole set of answers

sections.title: A boundary and a direction
sections.text: An inequality describes a set of values. The symbols < and > exclude the boundary; ≤ and ≥ include it. On a number line, use an open endpoint for a strict inequality and a closed endpoint for an included boundary.
sections.math: x<3\quad\text{means every real value less than }3
sections.example: Both 2 and −100 satisfy x < 3, but 3 does not. The solution is not just the largest integer below the boundary: real numbers such as 2.9 also qualify.

sections.title: Negative scaling reverses order
sections.text: Adding the same quantity preserves order. Multiplying or dividing by a positive number also preserves it. Multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses order because it reflects the number line.
sections.example: Since 2 < 5, multiplying by −1 gives −2 > −5. For −2x < 6, test x=0: 0<6 is true. It belongs to x>−3, not x<−3.

sections.title: Translate constraints precisely
sections.text: “At most” includes the maximum; “less than” excludes it. A real-valued solution set may need to be restricted to whole numbers in a counting problem. Test both a boundary value and a value away from it.
sections.example: A budget of $25 covers a $5 fee and $4 tickets. The inequality 5 + 4t ≤ 25 gives t ≤ 5. Since tickets are nonnegative whole numbers, the possible counts are 0,1,2,3,4,5.

sections.title: One output for each allowed input
sections.text: A function assigns exactly one output to each input in its domain. Different inputs may share an output. The notation f(x) names the output produced by input x; it does not mean f multiplied by x.
sections.example: The pairs {(1,4),(2,4),(3,7)} define a function on {1,2,3}. The pairs {(1,4),(1,6)} do not: input 1 has two outputs. A real function f(x)=1/x excludes zero from its domain.

sections.title: Slope measures change per input unit
sections.text: A linear function y = mx + b has constant slope m. Compute slope as the change in output divided by the corresponding nonzero change in input. Use the same point order in numerator and denominator. The intercept b is the output when x = 0.
sections.example: Through (2,7) and (5,13), m = (13−7)/(5−2) = 2. Substitute a point into y=2x+b: 7=4+b, so b=3. The rule is y=2x+3. A vertical line has zero input change, so its slope is undefined and it is not a function y of x.

sections.title: Distinguish linear from proportional
sections.text: A proportional relationship y = kx is a linear function with intercept zero. Constant rate alone does not make a relationship proportional. Interpret the slope and intercept in the units of the situation.
sections.example: A tank starts with 8 liters and fills at 3 liters per minute: V(t)=8+3t for t≥0 while the model remains valid. The slope is 3 liters per minute, and the intercept is the starting 8 liters. The relationship is linear but not proportional.

sections.title: Move between rule, table, and graph
sections.text: A graph is a set of input-output pairs. Evaluate a rule to build a table, and plot those pairs to see the relationship. Equal input steps produce equal output changes for a linear function. A finite table can suggest a rule, but does not uniquely determine every unobserved value unless a model class is specified.
sections.example: For y=2x+3, inputs −1,0,1,2 give outputs 1,3,5,7. Plot (−1,1),(0,3),(1,5),(2,7); all lie on a line. The output increases by 2 each time the input increases by 1.

activities.title: Find your starting point
activities.description: 8 questions · About 15 minutes · Ungraded prerequisite check. Your responses inform your learning record, but there is no passing score.

questions.prompt: Solve 3x + 7 = 22. What is x?
questions.solution: Subtract 7 to get 3x = 15, then divide by 3: x = 5.
questions.hint: Write the definition first. Check the units and denominator before calculating.

questions.prompt: Evaluate 1/2 + 1/3. Enter a decimal or fraction.
questions.solution: Use denominator 6: 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6.
questions.hint: Write the definition first. Check the units and denominator before calculating.

questions.prompt: Evaluate √49.
questions.solution: The nonnegative square root of 49 is 7.
questions.hint: Write the definition first. Check the units and denominator before calculating.

questions.prompt: If f(x) = 2x² − 1, find f(3).
questions.hint: Write the definition first. Check the units and denominator before calculating.

questions.prompt: A fair six-sided die is rolled. What is the probability of a result greater than 4?
questions.solution: Two of six equally likely outcomes, 5 and 6, qualify: 2/6 = 1/3.
questions.hint: Write the definition first. Check the units and denominator before calculating.

questions.prompt: If n changes from 4 to 16, what is the new value of 1/√n?
questions.hint: Write the definition first. Check the units and denominator before calculating.

questions.prompt: For x₁ = 2, x₂ = 5, x₃ = 8, evaluate Σᵢ₌₁³ xᵢ.
questions.solution: The notation means 2 + 5 + 8 = 15.
questions.hint: Write the definition first. Check the units and denominator before calculating.

questions.prompt: A fair coin has landed heads three times. Assuming independent tosses, what is P(heads next)?
questions.solution: Independence means previous results do not change the next toss probability.
questions.hint: Consider what the definition guarantees, and what requires additional assumptions.

activities.title: Week 1 · Core worksheet
activities.description: 18 problems · Work with notes · Numeric answers accept decimals or simple fractions. Written answers use a rubric after submission.

questions.prompt: Find the mean of {2,4,4,6}.
questions.hint: Write the definition first. Check the units and denominator before calculating.

questions.prompt: Find the mean of {1,2,9}.
questions.hint: Write the definition first. Check the units and denominator before calculating.

questions.prompt: For {1,2,9}, what is the deviation of 9 from the mean?
questions.hint: Write the definition first. Check the units and denominator before calculating.

questions.prompt: What is the sum of deviations from the mean for any finite nonempty dataset?
questions.solution: Σ(xᵢ − x̄) = Σxᵢ − nx̄ = 0.
questions.hint: Write the definition first. Check the units and denominator before calculating.

questions.prompt: For {2,4,4,6}, find the sum of squared deviations from the mean.
questions.hint: Write the definition first. Check the units and denominator before calculating.

questions.prompt: Treat {2,4,4,6} as the whole population. Find its variance.
questions.solution: Divide the sum 8 by population size 4: 2.
questions.hint: Write the definition first. Check the units and denominator before calculating.

questions.prompt: Treat {2,4,4,6} as a sample. Find its sample variance.
questions.solution: Divide 8 by n−1 = 3: 8/3.
questions.hint: Write the definition first. Check the units and denominator before calculating.

questions.prompt: Find the population standard deviation of {2,4,4,6}, to three decimals.
questions.solution: The square root of population variance 2 is about 1.414.
questions.hint: Write the definition first. Check the units and denominator before calculating.

questions.prompt: Measurements are in meters. In what units is variance measured?
questions.solution: Squaring deviations squares the units.
questions.hint: Consider what the definition guarantees, and what requires additional assumptions.

questions.prompt: Every observation increases by 10. The original variance is 7. What is the new variance?
questions.solution: Shifting every observation does not change deviations.
questions.hint: Write the definition first. Check the units and denominator before calculating.

questions.prompt: Y = −3X + 2 and X has SD 4. Find the SD of Y.
questions.solution: SD scales by |−3|: 3 × 4 = 12.
questions.hint: Write the definition first. Check the units and denominator before calculating.

questions.prompt: Y = 5 + 2X and X has mean 8. Find the mean of Y.
questions.hint: Write the definition first. Check the units and denominator before calculating.

questions.prompt: Find the z-score of 85 when the reference mean is 70 and SD is 10.
questions.hint: Write the definition first. Check the units and denominator before calculating.

questions.prompt: An observation has z = −2, reference mean 100, and SD 15. Find the observation.
questions.hint: Write the definition first. Check the units and denominator before calculating.

questions.prompt: Does standardizing a skewed distribution make it normal?
questions.solution: A linear rescaling preserves distribution shape.
questions.hint: Consider what the definition guarantees, and what requires additional assumptions.

questions.prompt: Explain why signed deviations cannot measure spread by their ordinary average. Give an example.
questions.solution: Deviations from the mean sum to zero, so their average is zero even for a spread-out dataset. For {1,3}, deviations −1 and 1 cancel.
rubric: State that deviations from the mean sum to zero.
Give a nonconstant dataset with cancelling deviations.
Explain why zero average deviation hides spread.
questions.hint: State the definitions, show each algebraic step, and explain the conclusion in words.

questions.prompt: Explain why sample variance uses n−1 rather than n when estimating population variance under independent identical sampling.
questions.solution: Fitting the mean makes the squared deviations too small on average. Their expectation is (n−1)σ², so dividing by n−1 yields an unbiased estimate.
rubric: Identify that the mean is estimated from the same sample.
Explain loss of one degree of freedom or downward bias.
Connect division by n−1 to unbiased estimation under the stated assumptions.
questions.hint: State the definitions, show each algebraic step, and explain the conclusion in words.

questions.prompt: A salary dataset has one exceptionally large value. Which best describes a typical salary without being pulled strongly by that value?
questions.solution: The median depends on rank and is less sensitive to a single extreme value.
questions.hint: Consider what the definition guarantees, and what requires additional assumptions.

activities.title: Week 1 · Derivations
activities.description: 4 written problems · Allow 30–45 minutes · Show each step before consulting the model solution.

questions.prompt: Prove Σᵢ(xᵢ − x̄) = 0 for n observations.
questions.solution: Σ(xᵢ − x̄) = Σxᵢ − nx̄. By definition x̄ = Σxᵢ/n, so the expression is zero.
rubric: Distribute the sum correctly.
Use the definition of x̄.
Conclude exactly zero.
questions.hint: State the definitions, show each algebraic step, and explain the conclusion in words.

questions.prompt: Prove Σᵢ(xᵢ − c)² = Σᵢ(xᵢ − x̄)² + n(x̄ − c)². Explain why the mean minimizes squared distance.
questions.solution: Write xᵢ−c = (xᵢ−x̄)+(x̄−c), expand squares, and sum. The cross term is 2(x̄−c)Σ(xᵢ−x̄)=0. The remaining n(x̄−c)² is nonnegative, with equality only at c=x̄.
rubric: Decompose each deviation.
Expand and eliminate the cross term.
Use nonnegativity to identify the unique minimizer.
questions.hint: State the definitions, show each algebraic step, and explain the conclusion in words.

questions.prompt: For yᵢ = a + bxᵢ, prove sᵧ² = b²sₓ² and sᵧ = |b|sₓ.
questions.solution: First ȳ=a+bx̄. Then yᵢ−ȳ=b(xᵢ−x̄). Square, sum, and divide by n−1. Taking nonnegative square roots gives |b|sₓ.
rubric: Derive the transformed mean.
Show transformed deviations and variance.
Explain the absolute value in standard deviation.
questions.hint: State the definitions, show each algebraic step, and explain the conclusion in words.

questions.prompt: For a dataset with positive population SD, prove the standardized values have population mean 0 and variance 1.
questions.solution: The standardized mean is Σ(xᵢ−μ)/(Nσ)=0. The variance is Σ((xᵢ−μ)/σ)²/N = σ²/σ²=1.
rubric: Use positive σ to justify division.
Show the standardized mean is zero.
Show the population variance is one.
questions.hint: State the definitions, show each algebraic step, and explain the conclusion in words.

activities.title: Week 1 · Check your understanding
activities.description: 8 questions · Suggested time: 20 minutes · Close your notes. No hints. Each question is equally weighted; written reasoning is self-assessed.

questions.prompt: Find the mean of {3,5,7,9}.
questions.hint: Write the definition first. Check the units and denominator before calculating.

questions.prompt: Treat {3,5,7,9} as a sample. Find the sample variance.
questions.solution: Deviations −3,−1,1,3 square to 9,1,1,9; sum 20. Divide by 3.
questions.hint: Write the definition first. Check the units and denominator before calculating.

questions.prompt: A population has variance 25. Find its standard deviation.
questions.hint: Write the definition first. Check the units and denominator before calculating.

questions.prompt: Y = 7 − 2X and X has variance 9. Find the variance of Y.
questions.hint: Write the definition first. Check the units and denominator before calculating.

questions.prompt: Find the z-score of 42 when the reference mean is 50 and SD is 4.
questions.hint: Write the definition first. Check the units and denominator before calculating.

questions.prompt: Without a distributional assumption, z = 2 tells you that an observation is…
options: Two SDs above the reference mean
questions.answer: Two SDs above the reference mean
questions.solution: Only the standardized distance is guaranteed.
questions.hint: Consider what the definition guarantees, and what requires additional assumptions.

questions.prompt: A friend averages signed deviations from the mean and gets zero. They conclude there is no variation. Explain the error.
questions.solution: Signed deviations always cancel around the mean, even for variable data. Use squared or absolute deviations to avoid cancellation.
rubric: Explain cancellation around the mean.
Distinguish zero signed average from zero variation.
Propose a valid spread measure.
questions.hint: State the definitions, show each algebraic step, and explain the conclusion in words.

questions.prompt: When would you divide squared deviations by N, and when by n−1? Explain the distinction.
questions.solution: Use N to describe the variance of the entire population of interest. Use n−1 for sample variance estimating a population variance under independent identical sampling; fitting the mean costs one degree of freedom.
rubric: Distinguish population description from estimation.
Assign each denominator correctly.
Explain fitting the mean or unbiasedness.
questions.hint: State the definitions, show each algebraic step, and explain the conclusion in words.
